Project 2: Spotify Songs' Genre Segmentation¶

Goal: Use the audio features of ~32k Spotify songs to (1) clean the data, (2) explore it visually, (3) inspect feature correlations, (4) cluster songs with K-Means and compare the clusters with playlist genres / playlist names, and (5) turn the result into a content-based song recommendation system.

In [1]:
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score, normalized_mutual_info_score
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', context='notebook')
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi']=100
RS=42

Findings & decisions

  • Only 5 rows have missing text fields (name/artist/album) → dropped.
  • 4,477 rows repeat a track_id: the same song sits in several playlists. For song-level clustering and recommendation we keep one row per song (otherwise popular songs are over-weighted and a song could be recommended to itself). The full table (df_all) is kept for the playlist-level analysis.
  • track_album_release_date is parsed to a release year, duration_ms converted to minutes.
In [4]:
df_all = raw.dropna().copy()
df_all['release_year'] = pd.to_datetime(df_all['track_album_release_date'], errors='coerce', format='mixed').dt.year
# some dates are year-only strings -> fall back to first 4 chars
df_all['release_year'] = df_all['release_year'].fillna(pd.to_numeric(df_all['track_album_release_date'].str[:4], errors='coerce'))
df_all['duration_min'] = df_all['duration_ms']/60000
df = df_all.drop_duplicates('track_id').reset_index(drop=True)
print('Rows (playlist entries):', len(df_all), '| unique songs:', len(df))
print('Missing release_year:', df.release_year.isna().sum())

Several features (speechiness, instrumentalness, liveness) are naturally skewed, so many points exceed the IQR fences – these are real songs (e.g. rap is highly speechy, ambient is highly instrumental), not errors. We keep them. The only clearly invalid rows would be tempo = 0 or extremely short tracks, handled below. Features are then standardised because K-Means is distance based and tempo/loudness live on much larger scales than the 0–1 features.

plt.figure(figsize=(11,4.5))

Insights: rap has the highest speechiness and danceability; EDM is the most energetic, loudest, fastest and least acoustic (and lowest in valence – darker/more intense mood); rock has the lowest danceability and speechiness; r&b is the most acoustic and the lowest in energy, loudness and tempo (the "calmest" genre); latin has the highest valence (happiest) together with high danceability; pop sits in the middle on most features.

3. Correlation matrix¶

In [15]:
num = audio+['track_popularity','key','mode']
corr = df[num].corr()
mask=np.triu(np.ones_like(corr,dtype=bool))
plt.figure(figsize=(11,8.5))
sns.heatmap(corr,mask=mask,annot=True,fmt='.2f',cmap='coolwarm',center=0,vmin=-1,vmax=1,square=True,linewidths=.5)
plt.title('Correlation matrix of Spotify audio features'); plt.show()
pairs=corr.where(~mask).stack().rename('r'); pairs=pairs[pairs.index.get_level_values(0)!=pairs.index.get_level_values(1)]
print('Strongest correlations:'); print(pairs.reindex(pairs.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index).head(8).round(2).to_string())

Strongest correlations:
loudness      energy              0.68
acousticness  energy             -0.55
              loudness           -0.37
valence       danceability        0.33
tempo         danceability       -0.19
speechiness   danceability        0.18
mode          key                -0.18
valence       instrumentalness   -0.17

Insights: energy and loudness are strongly positively correlated and both strongly negatively correlated with acousticness – loud tracks tend to be electric, not acoustic. valence correlates positively with danceability. Popularity has only very weak correlations with any audio feature (all |r| ≤ 0.12), so audio alone does not predict hits. Because no pair is close to ±1 (|r| < 0.8), we keep all features for clustering.

4. K-Means clustering¶

4.1 Choosing k (elbow + silhouette)¶

In [16]:
ks=range(2,11); inertia=[]; sil=[]
for k in ks:
    m=KMeans(k,n_init=10,random_state=RS).fit(X)
    inertia.append(m.inertia_); sil.append(silhouette_score(X,m.labels_,sample_size=8000,random_state=RS))
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(13,4))
ax[0].plot(ks,inertia,'o-'); ax[0].set_title('Elbow method'); ax[0].set_xlabel('k'); ax[0].set_ylabel('Inertia (WCSS)')
ax[1].plot(ks,sil,'o-',color='#C44E52'); ax[1].set_title('Silhouette score'); ax[1].set_xlabel('k')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

There is no sharp elbow and silhouette scores are low (≈0.12–0.17) at every k – songs form a continuum rather than well separated blobs, which is typical for audio-feature data. k = 2 scores highest but only splits "loud/energetic" vs "calm", which is too coarse for segmentation. We choose k = 6: it is a point where the inertia curve flattens, its silhouette is among the best for k ≥ 4, and it matches the six playlist genres so that the clusters can be directly compared with them.

In [17]:
K=6
km=KMeans(K,n_init=20,random_state=RS).fit(X)
df['cluster']=km.labels_
print('Silhouette (k=6, 8k sample):',round(silhouette_score(X,km.labels_,sample_size=8000,random_state=RS),3))
print(df.cluster.value_counts().sort_index().to_string())

Cluster summary (k = 6):

Cluster Sound profile Dominant genres
0 Happy, danceable, mid-tempo "feel-good" songs latin, pop, r&b
1 Acoustic, quiet, low-energy, longer tracks r&b, pop, rock
2 Long, energetic, instrumental, low-valence tracks EDM (57%)
3 Fast, loud, high-energy, less danceable rock, EDM, pop
4 Speech-heavy, danceable, upbeat, shorter tracks rap (57%)
5 Live-sounding, loud, high-energy, low danceability (smallest cluster) EDM, rock

Reading the result: the clusters line up with genres only partly (ARI ≈ 0.07, NMI ≈ 0.10). Two are clearly genre-driven – cluster 4 (rap) and cluster 2 (EDM) – while pop, latin and r&b share clusters because their audio profiles genuinely overlap. This is expected: Spotify's playlist genre is an editorial label, while K-Means groups songs purely by sound. The clusters are therefore more useful for finding similar-sounding songs than for re-predicting the label.

Playlist-level clustering (playlist names)¶

In [24]:
# Use every playlist entry (df_all): average the audio features of each playlist, then cluster playlists
pl=df_all.groupby(['playlist_name','playlist_genre'])[audio].mean().reset_index()
cnt=df_all.groupby(['playlist_name','playlist_genre']).size().rename('n').reset_index()
pl=pl.merge(cnt); pl=pl[pl.n>=5].reset_index(drop=True)
Xp=StandardScaler().fit_transform(pl[audio])
kp=KMeans(6,n_init=20,random_state=RS).fit(Xp); pl['pl_cluster']=kp.labels_
pp=PCA(2,random_state=RS).fit_transform(Xp); pl['pc1'],pl['pc2']=pp[:,0],pp[:,1]
print(len(pl),'playlists | ARI vs genre:',round(adjusted_rand_score(pl.playlist_genre,pl.pl_cluster),3),'| NMI:',round(normalized_mutual_info_score(pl.playlist_genre,pl.pl_cluster),3))
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(17,6.5))
sns.scatterplot(data=pl,x='pc1',y='pc2',hue='pl_cluster',palette='tab10',s=45,ax=ax[0]); ax[0].set_title('Playlists clustered by average audio features')
sns.scatterplot(data=pl,x='pc1',y='pc2',hue='playlist_genre',palette='Set2',s=45,ax=ax[1]); ax[1].set_title('Same playlists coloured by genre')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Clustering at the playlist level matches genre noticeably better than at the song level (ARI ≈ 0.27 vs 0.07): averaging many songs removes noise, so e.g. one cluster is almost all rap/trap playlists (RapCaviar, Hip-Hop Central, Trap 2020…), one is mostly EDM festival playlists and one mostly rock. Pop/latin/r&b playlists are still mixed together. One tiny cluster (3 playlists) is an outlier group.

6. Recommendation system¶

Approach (content-based): each song is a point in the standardised audio-feature space. For a chosen song we

  1. restrict candidates to the song's K-Means cluster (fast, same sound family), then
  2. rank them by cosine similarity of the feature vectors and return the top n (optionally boosted toward more popular songs and excluding the same artist).
In [26]:
feat_df=df.copy(); feat_df['key_']=feat_df.track_name.str.lower()
def recommend(song, artist=None, n=10, same_cluster=True, exclude_same_artist=False, min_pop=0):
    m=feat_df[feat_df.key_.str.contains(song.lower(),regex=False)]
    if artist: m=m[m.track_artist.str.lower().str.contains(artist.lower(),regex=False)]
    if m.empty: return f"Song '{song}' not found."
    q=m.sort_values('track_popularity',ascending=False).iloc[0]; qi=q.name
    pool=feat_df[feat_df.cluster==q.cluster] if same_cluster else feat_df
    pool=pool[(pool.index!=qi)&(pool.track_popularity>=min_pop)]
    if exclude_same_artist: pool=pool[pool.track_artist!=q.track_artist]
    sims=cosine_similarity(X[[qi]],X[pool.index])[0]
    out=pool.assign(similarity=sims).sort_values('similarity',ascending=False).drop_duplicates(['track_name','track_artist']).head(n)
    print(f"Query: {q.track_name} – {q.track_artist} | genre={q.playlist_genre} | cluster={q.cluster}\n")
    return out[['track_name','track_artist','playlist_genre','cluster','track_popularity','similarity']].round(3).reset_index(drop=True)
In [27]:
recommend('Shape of You', n=8, exclude_same_artist=True, min_pop=40)

Sanity check: do recommendations stay in the same genre?¶

In [30]:
rng=np.random.RandomState(RS); idx=rng.choice(len(df),500,replace=False); hit=[];hitc=[]
for i in idx:
    pool=np.where(df.cluster.values==df.cluster.values[i])[0]; pool=pool[pool!=i]
    s=cosine_similarity(X[[i]],X[pool])[0]; top=pool[np.argsort(-s)[:10]]
    hit.append((df.playlist_genre.values[top]==df.playlist_genre.values[i]).mean())
    s2=cosine_similarity(X[[i]],X)[0]; s2[i]=-1; top2=np.argsort(-s2)[:10]
    hitc.append((df.playlist_genre.values[top2]==df.playlist_genre.values[i]).mean())
print(f'Genre match of top-10 recs: within cluster {np.mean(hit):.1%} | whole catalogue {np.mean(hitc):.1%} | random baseline {(df.playlist_genre.value_counts(normalize=True)**2).sum():.1%}')

Genre match of top-10 recs: within cluster 39.6% | whole catalogue 39.8% | random baseline 16.8%

7. Conclusion¶

  • Pre-processing: removed 5 incomplete rows, collapsed duplicate songs (one row per track_id), engineered release year / duration in minutes, standardised 10 audio features.
  • EDA & correlation: genres have distinct audio fingerprints (rap → speechiness, EDM → energy/tempo/loudness, rock → low danceability, latin → high valence). Energy–loudness is strongly positive and both are strongly negative with acousticness; popularity is barely explained by audio features.
  • Clustering: K-Means with k = 6 (chosen via elbow + silhouette + interpretability) gives clusters with clear sonic identities. Song-level clusters only partly match playlist genres because genres overlap in sound; playlist-level clustering matches genre better (ARI 0.27 vs 0.07).
  • Recommender: cluster + cosine similarity returns similar-sounding songs; the top-10 lists match the query song's genre ~40% of the time vs ~17% by chance. Restricting to the cluster does not raise that rate compared with searching the whole catalogue (≈ 40% both), but it shrinks the search space and keeps results in the same sound family. Note the playlist_genre label is noisy (e.g. "Sweet Child O' Mine" is tagged pop), so genre match is only a rough proxy for quality.
  • Limitations / future work: silhouette is modest (songs form a continuum); only audio features are used – adding lyrics, artist and listening-history (collaborative filtering) would improve recommendations. Other algorithms (Gaussian Mixture, hierarchical, DBSCAN) could be compared.
